label: Chapter 2: The House of Luxembourg, 963 to 1443

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So for its first two centuries, the county was a modest affair.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A rocky fortress, a handful of villages, and a dynasty that married well and waited.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The counts of Luxembourg slowly gathered land, and in 1136 a stroke of inheritance gave the county to Henry the Blind, count of Namur, who joined the two territories together.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And his daughter was remarkable.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Ermesinde. She inherited the county in 1196 and ruled for more than fifty years, through two marriages and a great deal of politics.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She's remembered for granting charters of freedom to the towns of her county.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Including the capital.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1244, she gave one to the city of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It freed its townspeople from many of the old obligations of serfdom and let them organize themselves as a community, with a council of their own.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In a Europe where most people lived under their lord's thumb, that was a bold step.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To this day, Luxembourg treats Ermesinde as one of its founding figures.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Now the small county leaps onto the continental stage.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1288, the count of Luxembourg was killed at the Battle of Worringen, in a war over the succession to the neighboring duchy of Limburg.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His heir was a boy of about thirteen, also named Henry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We know him as Henry the Seventh.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And he grew up admired.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Chivalrous, pious, and quietly ambitious.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And in 1308, after the German king was murdered, the electors of the empire looked around for someone who was capable but not too powerful.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They chose the count of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's astonishing. A lord from a small county on the western edge.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Suddenly king of the Germans. And Henry seized the chance.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He arranged for his teenage son John to marry Elisabeth, the heiress of the kingdom of Bohemia, which is roughly today's Czech Republic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John became King of Bohemia in 1310.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In one stroke, the House of Luxembourg had acquired one of the richest crowns in central Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Henry himself?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He marched over the Alps into Italy, where he was crowned emperor in Rome in 1312.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He dreamed of restoring imperial glory.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The poet Dante, who lived through those years and pinned his hopes on Henry, wrote that a seat was waiting for him in Paradise.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But Henry died of a fever in 1313, near the city of Siena, and the dream died with him.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And his son John had a very different life.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Known to history as John the Blind, he was one of the great adventurers of the Middle Ages.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He was born in Luxembourg and raised partly at the French court.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As King of Bohemia, he was almost never home.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He fought in Italy, in Poland, and in Lithuania, alongside the crusading Teutonic Knights.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: He loved tournaments.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he loved France. His daughter Bonne married the man who would become King John the Second of France, and she became the grandmother of a future French king.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: When did he go blind?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By around 1340 he had lost his sight completely.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It didn't slow him down. In 1340 he founded a fair in Luxembourg City that still exists today, the Schueberfouer.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It takes place every year in late August and early September, with rides, food stalls, and traditional parades, and it's the biggest funfair in the country.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Then the war that defined his end.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1346, England and France were fighting what we now call the Hundred Years' War, and John, loyal to the French, rode to the battlefield of Crécy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Blind, he asked his knights to lead him into the fight.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: According to the old account, they tied their horses together by the reins, so that he wouldn't be separated, and charged straight into the English archers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the next morning.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John and his companions were found dead on the field.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the story about the feathers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Tradition says that the English prince, the one we call the Black Prince, who was just sixteen, took the three ostrich feathers from John's helmet as a trophy, and made them his own emblem.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians argue about whether that's really true.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But in Luxembourg, John is remembered as the great national hero.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His body now rests in the crypt of Notre-Dame cathedral in the capital, and to Luxembourgers he's a symbol of bravery, loyalty, and a certain doomed gallantry.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Now the greatest of the Luxembourgers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: John's eldest son. He was born in Prague and baptized with the name Wenceslas, but he took the name Charles at the French court, in honor of his godfather and uncle.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: As Charles the Fourth, he became King of Bohemia after his father's death, and in 1355 he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: He was a different kind of emperor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A scholar, a builder, and a patient politician.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1356 he issued a famous decree called the Golden Bull, which fixed how emperors would be elected by seven electors, a system that more or less lasted until the empire itself ended.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He founded Charles University in Prague in 1348, the first university in central Europe.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the bridge.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He started building the stone bridge across the Vltava that still bears his name.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He turned Prague into one of the great cities of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And he didn't forget the little county where his family began.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1354, Charles raised Luxembourg to the rank of duchy, and installed his half-brother Wenceslas as its first duke.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So by the late fourteenth century, this is a great dynasty.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its sons ruled Bohemia, and for a time Hungary, and sat on the imperial throne.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In all, four Luxembourgers held the title of ruler of the Holy Roman Empire: Henry the Seventh, Charles the Fourth, Charles's son Wenceslas the Fourth, and Charles's other son Sigismund.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Only three of them, Henry, Charles, and Sigismund, were actually crowned emperor in Rome.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Sigismund was the last.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A shrewd and restless man. He was King of Hungary from 1387, and he became King of the Romans in 1411.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He called the great Council of Constance, which met from 1414 to 1418 and ended a split in the Catholic Church, and which also burned the Czech reformer Jan Hus, an act that triggered the Hussite wars in Bohemia.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then the line ended.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Sigismund was crowned emperor in 1433, and he died in 1437.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He had no surviving son. With his death, the male line of the House of Luxembourg came to an end.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What happened to the little duchy in all this?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its glamorous rulers were scattered across central Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They spent most of their time in Prague, Buda, or Rome, and they rarely visited the place that had made them.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To them, Luxembourg was a source of money, and they treated it that way.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They mortgaged it. They pledged it as security for loans, and passed it around among cousins and creditors.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who ended up holding it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of them was a woman named Elisabeth of Görlitz, a niece of Sigismund.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: She was widowed, remarried, and constantly short of money.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the end, she sold her rights to the most powerful figure in the region: Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And that's how it passed to Burgundy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1443, his forces took possession of the city, reportedly by a surprise assault with the help of local nobles who were fed up with the unstable rule of the pledge-holders.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And just like that, the old era came to an end.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The county that had given Europe emperors and kings was now just one more piece in the growing Burgundian collection of lands.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Before we move on, there's a thread worth remembering.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The castles.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the countryside of Luxembourg, medieval lords built castles that still stand.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The most spectacular is Vianden, on a hill above a river in the north, one of the largest feudal residences in this part of Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the early fifteenth century, Vianden passed by inheritance to the family of Nassau, which would later become the Dutch royal house.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Keep that name in mind.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Four hundred years later, it'll be central to our story.
